description.value: The study investigated whether normally distributed endogenous testosterone levels are associated with behavioral emotion recognition and amygdala reactivity during explicit recognition of emotional facial expressions in healthy young males.

design.value: A group of 21 healthy right-handed young males underwent 3T functional MRI during an event-related explicit emotion recognition task involving five basic emotions and neutral facial expressions. Behavioral performance and blood testosterone levels were analyzed, and amygdala parameter estimates were examined using ROI and whole-slab analyses.

description.value: Subjects chose the correct emotion from two verbal possibilities presented on the left and right of each facial image by pressing the corresponding button.

Tasks engaging nonverbal intelligence, cognitive flexibility, visual learning and memory.

Blood samples were taken on the day of fMRI measurements and analyzed using an electrochemiluminescence-immunoassay (ECLIA); assay sensitivity was 0.2 ng/ml and intra-assay coefficient of variation was 4-8%.

description.value: Twenty-one right-handed healthy males aged 21-33 years were enrolled in the study. Participants were all students.

recruitment_method.value: recruited by advertisements at the University of Vienna and the Medical University of Vienna, Austria

medical_condition.value: healthy; no psychiatric disorders according to DSM IV

diagnostic_instrument.value: German version of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM (SCID)

medication_status.value: Only males without any hormone treatment were included; all participants had a negative drug screening.

education_summary.value: All participants were students; mean education 17.9 years, S.D. = 3.2.

task_description.value: The stimulus material consisted of 72 color photographs of facial expressions portraying an equal number of the five basic emotions—anger, disgust, fear, happiness and sadness—as well as neutral expressions. Subjects chose the correct emotion from two verbal possibilities presented on the left and right of the image by pressing the corresponding button with the right hand. Emotional facial expressions were presented for a maximum of 5 s with a variable interstimulus interval ranging from 12 to 18 s, during which subjects viewed a scrambled face with a central crosshair.

presentation_software.value: Presentation software package (Neurobehavioral Systems Inc., Albany, CA, USA)

instructions.value: Subjects were instructed to choose the correct emotion from two verbal possibilities presented on the left and right of the image.

stimuli.value: 72 color photographs of facial expressions portraying anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral expressions, with female and male posers.

instrument.value: 3 Tesla Medspec whole-body scanner (Bruker Biospin, Ettlingen, Germany) at the MR Centre of Excellence, Medical University of Vienna, Austria

description.value: Echo-planar-imaging protocol optimized for measuring amygdala activation, using gradient-recalled EPI with 10 oblique axial slices centered on the amygdala, asymmetric k-space sampling, FOV = 25 cm × 21 cm, matrix size 128 × 91, slice thickness 2 mm, slice gap 0.5 mm, TR = 1000 ms and TE = 31 ms.

Functional data were preprocessed using SPM2. Images were slice timing corrected, realigned to the mean image, normalized into standardized stereotactic space, and spatially smoothed using an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a full-width-at-half-maximum of 9 mm.

steps.value: spatial smoothing using an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a full-width-at-half-maximum of 9 mm

hrf_model.value: canonical hemodynamic response function and its temporal derivative

model_settings.value: Each stimulus was modelled with a separate regressor based on the individual response period; regressors of each valence were pooled to assess brain responses to each emotion, leaving a minimum of 12 stimuli per category.

Contrast images from all subjects were included in a second level random effects analysis. Emotion and gender of poser were within-subject factors. Whole-slab and direct-comparison results were presented at p < .001 uncorrected.

Mean parameter estimates were extracted for left and right amygdala ROI in each condition at p < .001 uncorrected. Emotion, gender of poser and laterality were applied as repeated factors. Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-values are presented.

Recognition accuracy and reaction time were analyzed with emotion and gender of poser as within-subjects factors. Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-values were used for all ANOVAs and post hoc results were Bonferroni corrected.

For each emotion, testosterone level was correlated with mean parameter estimates within the amygdala provided by ROI analyses across all participants; results were corrected for multiple correlations.
Voxelwise correlation analyses tested associations of testosterone with activation during angry male and fearful male expressions.
